items.prose: A research group plans a tied GPT with vocabulary 50,257, context 2,048, width 2,048, 24 blocks and a 4 times wider MLP, trained on 1 trillion tokens.

parts.question: How many parameters does the model have, biases and norms included?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the two embedding tables, 24 blocks and the closing layer norm.

byKey.untied: The model is tied; no separate head.

parts.question: Using the 1,315,723,264 parameters of part 1, what is the training compute, in units of $10^{21}$ FLOPs? Give 2 decimal places.
Taking 7.89 $\times 10^{21}$ FLOPs, how many days on 64 GPUs of 312 TFLOP/s peak at 45% utilisation? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: Divide by $64 \times 3.12 \times 10^{14} \times 0.45$ FLOP/s and by 86,400: about 10.2 days.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide by the achieved rate, then by the seconds in a day.

explain.text: Together the 64 GPUs deliver $8.99 \times 10^{15}$ FLOP/s; the run needs 878,555 seconds of that, 10.2 days.

parts.question: At £1.80 per GPU-hour, what does a run of 10.2 days on 64 GPUs cost? Give the answer in pounds to the nearest hundred.

feedback.generic: Not quite. GPU-hours times the rate.

items.prose: A pilot trains two models of a new family: $10^8$ parameters reach a held-out loss of 3.0 and $10^9$ reach 2.6.

parts.question: What exponent $\alpha$ do the two runs give for $L = aN^{-\alpha}$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the change in log loss by the change in log size.

byKey.lin: That is the drop in loss on linear axes.
byKey.ln: You used $\ln$ for the loss but $\log_{10}$ for the size: one decade is $\ln 10$ in natural logs.

explain.text: One decade, and the loss ratio 3.0/2.6: $\alpha = \log_{10}(1.1538) \approx 0.0621$.

parts.question: Using $\alpha = 0.0621$ from part 1, what loss does the law predict at $10^{10}$ parameters? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply 2.6 by the per-decade factor.

byKey.lin: You extended the drop of 0.4 linearly. The law multiplies.

explain.text: The factor per decade is $2.6/3.0$, so $2.6 \times 2.6/3.0 \approx 2.2533$.

parts.question: Why is that prediction weak evidence?

options.text: Two points always fit; the step leaves the data
Only because the two losses are noisy
options.why: Noise matters, but two points cannot test the law at all.

options.text: Because the floor of the law is known
options.why: The floor is unknown here, which makes it worse.

feedback.correct: Two points always fit, and $10^{10}$ is outside the pilot.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Can two points test a power law?

explain.text: Fit more sizes, and expect a floor to flatten the curve.

items.prose: A team has $10^{22}$ FLOPs and follows the headline rule of 20 tokens per parameter.

parts.question: With $D = 20N$ and $C = 6ND$, $C = 120N^2$. How many parameters should the model have, in billions? Give 2 decimal places.

byKey.no-twenty: You solved $6N^2 = C$, leaving out the 20 tokens per parameter.

parts.question: Using the 9.13 billion parameters of part 1, how many tokens, in billions? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Twenty tokens per parameter.

parts.question: The model will answer millions of queries a day. Which change makes sense?

options.text: A smaller model on more tokens, cheaper to serve
A larger model on fewer tokens
options.why: That raises the cost of every query.

options.text: Keep the 20-tokens split whatever the use

feedback.correct: Serving cost scales with $N$, so heavy use favours a smaller model trained longer.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which split is cheaper per query?

explain.text: Each query costs about $2N$ FLOPs per token, so a smaller, longer-trained model pays back over many queries.
